NALT's Blue Book Basic Guide: An Overview of its Purpose and Scope

The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide for Legal Research Writing in Nigeria, also known as the NALT's Blue Book Basic Guide, is a critical document for the Nigerian legal academic community. It serves as a nationally approved uniform format and citation guide for legal research intended for law faculties and legal research institutes in Nigeria. This manual, published by the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT), aims to standardize legal research and writing practices across the nation.

Purpose:

The primary purpose of the NALT's Blue Book is to address the historical lack of a dedicated, uniform format and citation guide specifically tailored for legal research writing in Nigeria. Before its development, Nigerian Law Faculties commonly utilized various foreign citation styles such as OSCOLA, MLA, APA, and Bluebook, which often proved inadequate for addressing specific Nigerian legal research needs. This reliance on foreign styles led to a lack of uniformity and coherence in legal scholarship across different institutions.

To remedy these issues, the NALT's Blue Book was created with the following key objectives:

To bridge the existing gaps in research formats and establish a uniform approach to research writing and citation within Nigerian law faculties and research institutes.

To promote uniformity and coherence in legal technical writing within the Nigerian legal academic profession.

To provide a customised standard format and reference guide that is indigenous to legal research writing in Nigeria.

To serve as a comprehensive guide for students' project writing at all levels (undergraduate and postgraduate) and to assist academic legal researchers in their scholarly activities, particularly in preparing articles for journal publication.

To address the perennial challenges of poor presentation in both undergraduate and postgraduate research projects.

To alleviate the difficulties faced by external examiners in navigating the diverse writing formats prevalent across different campuses.

To 'Nigerianise' referencing by prioritizing local cases, statutes, and academic authors while retaining valuable technical features from styles like OSCOLA.

To facilitate the compulsory teaching of legal research methodology in higher education and relevant legal research institutes in Nigeria.

Ultimately, the NALT's Blue Book aims to elevate the quality and standard of legal research in Nigeria, fostering a more unified and locally relevant body of legal scholarship.

Scope:

The NALT's Blue Book Basic Guide is designed to be all-encompassing, covering a broad spectrum of elements essential for conducting and presenting legal research. Its scope is structured around four major parts:

Part One: Background Information to NALT Format: This introductory section provides the historical context of the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide, detailing its development from the initial proposal in 2013 to its ratification at ABUAD in 2015. It lays the foundation for understanding the rationale and aspirations behind the guide.

Part Two: NALT Format and the Structuring of Research Topics: This crucial part focuses on the practical aspects of structuring legal research writing. It outlines the two main approaches to legal research in Nigeria: doctrinal (conceptual/library-based) and non-doctrinal (empirical/socio-legal). It provides guidelines for structuring research topics into chapters for undergraduate long essays (typically five chapters, 50-100 pages), master's dissertations (typically five chapters, 100-150 pages), and PhD theses (typically six chapters, 200-400 pages). This section also covers essential preliminaries such as the title page, abstract (with specific word counts: one page for undergraduate and postgraduate, 200-250 words for journal articles), bibliography, and appendices. It provides guidance on font (Times New Roman, size 12), spacing (double, except for abstract), margins, and pagination.

Part Three: NALT Citation Guidelines for Style of Referencing: This core section provides detailed rules and examples for citing various legal sources according to the NALT standard. It covers the citation of primary sources like Nigerian statutes (including the Constitution) and case law, as well as secondary sources such as textbooks, journal articles, monographs, lecture notes, conference papers/proceedings, newspapers, theses, online sources, and lectures. The NALT style adopts the footnote method for referencing and provides guidance on abbreviations, punctuation, the use of 'ibid.' and cross-referencing '(n...)', handling quotations, and the preparation of the bibliography, highlighting its differences from footnotes.

Part Four: Format for Articles in Journal for Publication: This section offers specific guidelines for structuring articles intended for submission to academic journals. It outlines the recommended structure with sub-main titles (using Arabic numerals) and sub-subtitles (using lowercase letters with initial capitals), as well as requirements for the title (concise, 13-18 words, capitalised and centralised), author information (including footnotes for affiliations), abstract (not more than 200-250 words, single-spaced), keywords (not more than 5, alphabetical), the body of the article (indented paragraphs), findings, recommendations, conclusion, length limitations (15-20 pages including abstract and footnotes), font (Times New Roman 12, 1.5 spacing), paragraphing, handling of quotations (less than 3 lines in text with single quotes), and the crucial requirement that all citations must adhere to the NALT format. Footnotes in articles should be in Times New Roman font size 10.

The NALT's Blue Book is intended to be a user-friendly resource for a wide audience, including law students at all levels, law teachers, and even non-legal researchers in related disciplines like Arts, Social Sciences, and Humanities. By providing a comprehensive and localized framework for legal research and citation, the NALT aims to significantly contribute to the advancement of legal scholarship in Nigeria.

NALT Citation Guide: Developing Your Research Core (Chapters 3, 4 and 5)

Building upon the foundational work of Chapter Two (Framework & Literature Review), the subsequent chapters – Chapters Three, Four, and Five (or Three, Four, and Six for PhD theses) – form the core of your legal research under the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide. These chapters are where you delve into the substance of your research, present your analysis, and articulate your findings. The structure and content of these chapters will vary depending on whether you adopt a doctrinal or non-doctrinal approach.

The Doctrinal Approach: In-Depth Analysis and Conclusion

Under the doctrinal approach, which is described as purely qualitative and often library/online-based, Chapters Three and Four provide the space for thorough examination and critical analysis of your main research topic. The NALT guide offers flexibility in structuring these chapters for undergraduate and master's dissertations, allowing candidates to distribute their topics freely within these two chapters. For PhD theses, Chapters Three, Four, and Five are at the candidate's discretion, under the guidance of their supervisors.

Chapter Three: This chapter typically represents the re-statement of your main research topic or the subject matter for in-depth analysis. It's often the largest of the chapters in master's and PhD legal research under the doctrinal approach. For example, if your topic is "THE ANALYSIS OF LEGAL AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS FOR HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA," Chapter Three might be titled "LEGAL AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS FOR HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA" and further explore specific legal frameworks like international and domestic provisions.

Chapter Four: This chapter can serve as a continuation of the analysis from Chapter Three, addressing the application and enforcement of the topic under discussion. It can also focus on the problems and challenges associated with your research topic. Using the human trafficking example, Chapter Four might analyze the "CHALLENGES IN THE APPLICATION AND ENFORCEMENT OF HUMAN TRAFFICKING LAWS IN NIGERIA" and explore various forms of trafficking and their effects. You can utilize sub-titles and sub-sub-titles, using numerical or alphabetical ordering to logically present related topics. The key is to cluster related topics rather than creating artificial boundaries with unnecessary additional chapters.

Chapter Five (or Six for PhD): Concluding Your Research

The final chapter, which is Chapter Five for undergraduate and master's dissertations and Chapter Six for PhD theses, is dedicated to the Conclusion. The NALT guide specifies a uniform structure for this chapter across all levels of study. It typically includes the following sections:

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS: A concise recap of the key discoveries and insights derived from your research.

RECOMMENDATIONS: Practicable suggestions based on your findings that address the problems identified in your research. Avoid unrealistic recommendations.

CONTRIBUTIONS TO KNOWLEDGE: An articulation of the specific ways your research adds to the existing body of knowledge in your field.

AREAS FOR FURTHER STUDIES: Suggestions for potential future research that could build upon or extend your work.

CONCLUSION: A final statement that brings your research to a close, summarizing your main arguments and their significance.

The Non-Doctrinal Approach: Empirical Investigation and Findings

For those employing a non-doctrinal (empirical/socio-legal) approach, which involves scientific investigation and data collection through fieldwork, the structure of Chapters Three, Four, and Five differs significantly. While the overall thesis structure remains at six chapters for PhD, the focus of the middle chapters shifts.

Chapter Three: Research Methodology: This chapter is unique to the non-doctrinal approach and details the methods used for data collection. It should cover aspects such as research design, population sampling, and specific research techniques like interviews, questionnaires, and experimental designs.

Chapters Four and Five: Data Analysis, Presentation of Results, and Discussions: These chapters are devoted to the analysis of the collected data, the presentation of the research findings, and a discussion of the results in relation to your research questions or hypotheses. Chapter Four may present the analyzed data, while Chapter Five offers a discussion of the findings, including their implications, limitations, and relationship to existing literature. For a PhD, the content of Chapter Four for a Master's might be split into Chapters Four and Five.

Chapter Six (for PhD using Non-Doctrinal Approach): Conclusion

Similar to the doctrinal approach, the final chapter for a PhD using the non-doctrinal approach is Chapter Six: Conclusion. It follows a similar structure, including a summary of findings, recommendations, contribution to knowledge, suggested areas for further studies, and a concluding remark.

Consistent Application of the NALT Citation Guide

Regardless of whether you choose a doctrinal or non-doctrinal approach, it is absolutely essential to consistently apply the NALT citation guide throughout Chapters Three, Four (and Five where applicable). Every source you refer to, whether primary legal materials, academic literature, or empirical data, must be meticulously cited using the footnote style prescribed in Part Three of the NALT manual. This includes proper formatting for case citations, statutes, books, journal articles, and other relevant materials. Remember that footnote citations should be in full.

By carefully developing the content and structure of Chapters Three, Four, and Five (or Six), while adhering strictly to the NALT citation guidelines, you will construct a robust and credible body of work that effectively addresses your research objectives and contributes meaningfully to legal scholarship in Nigeria.

NALT Citation Guide: Mastering the 5-Chapter Structure for Nigerian Master's Dissertations

For Master's degree candidates in Nigerian law faculties, the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides a crucial framework for structuring your dissertation. Adhering to this structure is essential for a well-organized and academically sound research project. This post will guide you through mastering the NALT-recommended 5-chapter structure for your Master's dissertation.

The NALT Standard: A 5-Chapter Framework

According to the NALT guide, the body of a Master's dissertation is divided into five chapters. This structure, primarily discussed under the doctrinal (conceptual/library-based) legal research approach, aims to ensure a uniform and logical presentation of research. While the non-doctrinal approach exists with a slightly different structure, the 5-chapter format is a cornerstone of the NALT guidelines for Master's dissertations.

The Mandatory Chapters: Setting the Foundation and Concluding Your Work

The NALT guide emphasizes that Chapters One, Two, and Five are mandatory and should be structured in a consistent manner by all Master's candidates, regardless of their specific research topic.

CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION

This chapter is highly technical and crucial as it anchors the entire research. It typically includes:

BACKGROUND TO THE STUDY

STATEMENT OF PROBLEM (followed by Research Questions)

AIM AND OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY

RESEARCH METHODOLOGY

CHAPTERS ANALYSIS (a synopsis of the contents of each chapter)

CHAPTER TWO: CONCEPTUAL, THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS AND LITERATURE REVIEW

This chapter lays the intellectual groundwork for your research and comprises three or four major parts:

Conceptual Framework: Defining the key concepts relevant to your topic.

Theoretical Framework: Discussing the theories that underpin your research.

Literature Review: A critical analysis of existing scholarly works (journals, books, articles) related to your research topic, emphasizing peer-reviewed journals. This section should explain how previous studies build on or depart from your current research and how your research offers a unique perspective.

CHAPTER FIVE: CONCLUSION

This is the final chapter and typically includes:

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS

RECOMMENDATIONS

CONTRIBUTIONS TO KNOWLEDGE

AREAS FOR FURTHER STUDIES

CONCLUSION (a final statement summarizing your research)

Chapters Three and Four: Flexibility in Developing Your Core Arguments

The NALT guide grants candidates discretion in structuring Chapters Three and Four to address their main research topic thoroughly. It is advised that students begin addressing their main topic from Chapter Three.

For example, if your research topic is: ‘THE ANALYSIS OF LEGAL AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS FOR HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA’, Chapters Three and Four could be structured as follows:

CHAPTER THREE: LEGAL AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS FOR HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA

3.1 LEGAL FRAMEWORKS FOR HUMAN TRAFFICKING

3.1.1 INTERNATIONAL PROVISIONS

3.1.2 NATIONAL STATUTES

3.1.3 OTHER PROVISIONS (if any)

3.2 INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORKS

3.2.1 (Sub-titles for specific institutions)

CHAPTER FOUR: HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA: CAUSES AND EFFECTS

4.1 CAUSES OF HUMAN TRAFFICKING

4.1.1 PUSH FACTORS

4.1.2 PULL FACTORS

4.2 FORMS AND PATTERNS OF HUMAN TRAFFICKING

4.2.1 SEXUAL EXPLOITATION

4.2.2 FORCED LABOUR/SERVITUDE

(and other relevant forms)

4.3 EFFECTS OF HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN NIGERIA

(Further breakdown as needed)

Remember that these are illustrative examples, and the specific content and sub-sections of Chapters Three and Four will depend entirely on your research topic and under the guidance of your supervisor. Chapters Three or Four can be further divided into more sub-titles using Arabic numerals, and sub-sub-titles can be indicated using lowercase letters or Roman numerals.

Beyond the Chapters: Preliminaries and Bibliography

The five main chapters are preceded by preliminaries (numbered in Roman numerals) and followed by the bibliography and appendices (if any). The preliminaries typically include the title page, declaration, certification, acknowledgements, table of contents, lists of cases, statutes, abbreviations, and the abstract. The bibliography lists all the sources you consulted, formatted according to the specific NALT guidelines discussed in our previous conversation.

A Note on Non-Doctrinal Approaches

While this post focuses on the 5-chapter structure common in doctrinal research, it's important to note that the non-doctrinal (empirical/socio-legal) approach may involve a slightly different structure, particularly with a dedicated chapter on Research Methodology (Chapter Three). However, even in this approach, the total number of chapters for a Master's dissertation remains five, and the Introduction and Conclusion chapters generally retain similar content.

Conclusion: Structuring for Success

Mastering the NALT's 5-chapter structure is a fundamental step towards producing a well-organized, coherent, and academically rigorous dissertation in Nigerian law faculties. By understanding the mandatory content of Chapters One, Two, and Five, and strategically planning the content of Chapters Three and Four to address your research topic, you will lay a strong foundation for a successful Master's degree.

Always consult the official NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide for detailed and specific instructions.

NALT Citation Guide: Navigating the 6-Chapter PhD Thesis Structure in Nigeria

For doctoral candidates in Nigerian law faculties, the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides a structured roadmap for crafting a comprehensive and impactful thesis. A key aspect of this guide is the NALT-recommended 6-chapter structure for PhD theses. This post will serve as your guide to understanding and navigating this essential framework.

The NALT Standard: A 6-Chapter Framework for Doctoral Research

According to the NALT guide, a PhD thesis in law is divided into six main chapters. This structure is primarily discussed within the context of the doctrinal (conceptual/library-based) legal research approach. While a non-doctrinal (empirical/socio-legal) approach also exists, the 6-chapter format is a central element of the NALT guidelines for PhD theses.

The Cornerstone Chapters: Introduction, Foundations, and Conclusion

The NALT guide clearly states that Chapters One, Two, and Six are mandatory and must follow a consistent structure across all PhD theses, irrespective of the specific research area.

CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION

This foundational chapter sets the stage for your entire research project and typically encompasses:

BACKGROUND TO THE STUDY

STATEMENT OF PROBLEM (followed by clearly articulated Research Questions, with a maximum of five or six)

AIM AND OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY

RESEARCH METHODOLOGY

CHAPTERS ANALYSIS (a detailed synopsis outlining the content of each of the six chapters)

CHAPTER TWO: CONCEPTUAL, THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS AND LITERATURE REVIEW

This crucial chapter establishes the intellectual context of your research through:

CONCEPTUAL CLARIFICATIONS: Defining and explaining the key terms and concepts central to your research topic.

THEORETICAL AND HISTORICAL FOUNDATION: Discussing the relevant jurisprudential bases, theories, principles, and historical context that inform your study.

LITERATURE REVIEW: A comprehensive and critical analysis of existing scholarly works (including peer-reviewed journals, books, and articles) that are relevant to your research. This section should demonstrate your understanding of the current state of knowledge, identify gaps in the literature, and explain how your research builds upon or departs from previous studies, offering a unique perspective.

CHAPTER SIX: CONCLUSION

This final chapter brings your research to a close by providing:

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS: A concise overview of the key outcomes of your research.

RECOMMENDATIONS: Based on your findings, suggesting practical or policy-oriented actions.

CONTRIBUTIONS TO KNOWLEDGE: Highlighting the novel insights and additions your research makes to the existing body of legal scholarship.

AREAS FOR FURTHER STUDIES: Suggesting potential avenues for future research arising from your work.

CONCLUSION: A final statement that succinctly summarizes the main arguments and significance of your thesis.

Chapters Three, Four, and Five: Developing Your Core Analysis

The NALT guide provides PhD candidates with flexibility in structuring Chapters Three, Four, and Five to allow for in-depth exploration and analysis of their specific research topic. It is generally advised to begin the main analysis of your topic in Chapter Three.

Depending on your research focus and methodology, these chapters could be structured in various ways. For instance, if your research topic is ‘THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW IN NIGERIA’:

CHAPTER THREE: THEORETICAL UNDERPINNINGS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW

(Exploring the relevant theoretical frameworks in both fields)

CHAPTER FOUR: ANALYSIS OF THE APPLICATION OF EXISTING NIGERIAN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAWS TO AI-GENERATED WORKS

(Examining the challenges and limitations of current laws)

CHAPTER FIVE: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF INTERNATIONAL APPROACHES TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY PROTECTION FOR AI-GENERATED WORKS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR NIGERIA

(Drawing lessons from other jurisdictions and proposing solutions)

Alternatively, under a non-doctrinal approach, Chapter Three would typically be dedicated to RESEARCH METHODOLOGY, detailing the methods used for data collection and analysis. Chapters Four and Five would then focus on research analysis and data presentation.

It is crucial to work closely with your supervisor to determine the most logical and effective structure for these central analytical chapters of your thesis. You can further break down the topics within these chapters into sub-titles and sub-sub-titles using Arabic numerals, lowercase letters, or Roman numerals to ensure a well-organized and coherent presentation.

The Broader Structure: Preliminaries and Bibliography

The six main chapters are situated within a broader framework that includes preliminaries (numbered using Roman numerals) at the beginning and the bibliography and appendices (if any) at the end. The preliminaries generally consist of the blank fly leaf, title page, declaration page, certification page, acknowledgements, table of contents, lists of cases, statutes, abbreviations, and a comprehensive abstract (not exceeding 500-600 words). The bibliography provides a complete list of all sources consulted in your research, formatted according to the specific NALT citation guidelines.

Conclusion: Building a Robust Doctoral Argument

Adhering to the NALT's 6-chapter structure is fundamental for developing a well-structured, logically sound, and impactful PhD thesis in Nigerian law. By understanding the mandatory components of Chapters One, Two, and Six, and thoughtfully planning the content of Chapters Three, Four, and Five in consultation with your supervisor, you will establish a strong and coherent framework for your doctoral research journey.

NALT Citation Guide: Structuring Your Nigerian Law Undergraduate Long Essay

Welcome to your guide on structuring your undergraduate long essay in Nigerian Law, following the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide for Legal Research Writing in Nigeria (NALT’s Blue Book Basic Guide). This manual is a nationally approved uniform format and citation guide designed for law faculties and legal research institutes in Nigeria. Adhering to its guidelines will ensure your research paper meets the required academic standards within the Nigerian legal education system.

Understanding the NALT Framework for Your Long Essay

The NALT guide aims to provide a standardized approach to legal research writing in Nigeria. For undergraduate long essays, it specifies a clear structure to help you present your research in a logical and coherent manner. The goal is to address the perennial problems of poor presentations of undergraduate research projects.

The Core Structure: Five Chapters

According to the NALT guide, the body of your undergraduate long essay is divided into five main chapters. These chapters are preceded by preliminary pages and conclude with a bibliography and appendices (if any). This structure is designed to ensure a logical flow of your arguments and analysis.

I. Preliminary Pages (Numbered in Roman Numerals)

The preliminary section of your long essay should include the following, numbered using Roman numerals:

The Blank Fly Leaf: This is the very first page and should be blank.

The Title Page: This page contains essential information such as the approved title of your essay (in uppercase), your full name, matriculation number, any qualifications held, and the submission details to your faculty and university for the award of your degree (see specific examples in the NALT guide). No page number is indicated on the title page, although it is considered page i, and the actual numbering starts from page ii. All items on the title page are capitalized.

The Declaration Page: This is where you formally declare that the work is your own original effort. This is page ii.

Certification Page: This page usually confirms that your supervisor has approved your work for submission.

Dedication (Optional): You may choose to dedicate your work.

Acknowledgements: Here, you can express gratitude to those who supported your research.

Table of Contents: This provides an overview of your essay's structure, including chapters, sub-titles, and sub-sub-titles with their corresponding page numbers. All titles and items in the table of contents are in uppercase.

List of Cases (if any): If you have a significant number of cases, list them in alphabetical order.

List of Statutes, Treaties, and Other International Instruments (if any): Similarly, list these in alphabetical order if applicable.

List of Acronyms/Abbreviations (if any): If you use acronyms or abbreviations, provide a list in alphabetical order.

Abstract: This is a non-paragraphed summary of your essay, typically between 200-350 words. It should be in the same font as the body but with single line spacing. The abstract is usually located as the last page of the preliminaries before Chapter One.

II. The Body: Five Core Chapters (Numbered in Arabic Numerals)

The main body of your long essay consists of five chapters, numbered using Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3...). Each chapter must have a title presented in uppercase (capital letters) with no number assigned. Main titles under the chapter title are also in uppercase but must be assigned a number in Arabic numerals, while sub-titles and sub-sub-titles use sub-Arabic numerals.

While the specific content of Chapters Three and Four will depend on your research topic, Chapters One, Two, and Five are structured in a similar way by all students, irrespective of the topic.

CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION: This chapter sets the stage for your research. It typically includes elements such as:

BACKGROUND TO THE STUDY

STATEMENT OF PROBLEM (followed by Research Questions)

AIM AND OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY

RESEARCH METHODOLOGY (A brief overview of how you conducted your research)

CHAPTERS ANALYSIS (A brief synopsis of the contents of each chapter)

CHAPTER TWO: CONCEPTUAL, THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS AND LITERATURE REVIEW: This chapter provides the foundational understanding for your research. It generally includes:

CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK: Defining and explaining key terms and issues relevant to your research. This can be further broken down (e.g., 2.1.1 DEFINITION OF TERMS).

THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: Explaining the relevant jurisprudential basis, theories, and principles that underpin your study.

LITERATURE REVIEW: Discussing existing published works, opinions of authorities, and results of previous studies related to your topic. This section analyzes and synthesizes relevant scholarship.

CHAPTER THREE & FOUR: These chapters are where you delve into the main analysis and discussion of your research topic. The titles and content of these chapters will be specific to your research question. You can break down your main topic into logical sub-themes and analyze them in these chapters, using sub-titles and sub-sub-titles as needed.

CHAPTER FIVE: SUMMARY, RECOMMENDATIONS, AND CONCLUSION: This final chapter brings your research to a close. It typically includes:

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS

RECOMMENDATIONS (based on your findings)

CONTRIBUTIONS TO KNOWLEDGE (highlighting the unique contributions of your research)

AREAS FOR FURTHER STUDIES

CONCLUSION (a concise concluding statement that summarizes your main arguments and findings)

III. Concluding Pages

BIBLIOGRAPHY: This is a systematic listing of all the published works you consulted (books, journals, articles, cases, statutes, etc.) arranged in a specific order. The NALT guide has specific rules for formatting your bibliography, including the order of author names and the presentation of different types of sources. Bibliography starts with the author's surname. Remember the key differences between footnotes and the bibliography in terms of author name order and inclusion of page numbers.

APPENDICES (if any): These may include supplementary materials that are relevant to your research but not essential to the main body of your essay, such as questionnaires, interview transcripts, or statistical data. Appendices are placed on separate pages after the bibliography.

Formatting Requirements

Adhere to the following formatting guidelines as outlined by the NALT guide:

Font: Times New Roman

Font Size: 12

Spacing: Double spacing for the main body of the text

Paper: White, good quality, size A4. Only one side of the paper should be used for typing.

Margins: Specific margins are prescribed (Top: 25mm, Bottom: 12mm, Right: 13mm, Left: 38mm) to allow for binding.

Pagination: Preliminary pages are numbered with Roman numerals (ii onwards), and the main body with Arabic numerals (1 onwards). Page numbers are located at the bottom, centrally located.

Paragraphing: The dissertation/thesis should be typed double-spaced.

Footnotes: The NALT citation guide for footnotes shall be adopted within the text for both sources consulted and for plausible explanations of words without interrupting the flow of the essay. Footnotes should be in single line spacing and en-blocked (no paragraphing). Remember that footnote citations should generally be in full.

The Importance of Uniformity

By following these guidelines from the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide, you contribute to a uniform and standardized approach to legal research writing in Nigeria. This not only enhances the quality and coherence of legal scholarship but also facilitates the assessment of research work by both internal and external examiners.

Remember to consult the full NALT guide for detailed examples and specific instructions on citation styles for various legal and non-legal sources. Good luck with your long essay!

NALT Citation Guide: Understanding Chapter Two (Framework & Literature Review) in Nigeria

This post explores Chapter Two: Conceptual, Theoretical Frameworks and Literature Review within the context of legal research in Nigeria, following the guidelines of the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide. This chapter holds significant importance, particularly in postgraduate legal research, as it provides the essential intellectual foundation for your study.

The Role of Chapter Two: Establishing the Intellectual Context

The NALT manual identifies Chapter Two, often titled ‘Conceptual, Theoretical Frameworks and Literature Review’, as crucial for building the intellectual bedrock of both master’s dissertations and PhD theses. A well-developed Chapter Two showcases your grasp of existing scholarly work, the fundamental theories that inform your research, and the key concepts inherent in your chosen legal domain. The manual also notes that a meticulously prepared research proposal, adhering to all technical specifications, essentially encompasses the content of the initial two chapters of a PhD thesis.

Key Components of Chapter Two (Doctrinal Approach)

Under the doctrinal approach to legal research writing, Chapter Two generally consists of three or four primary sections:

CONCEPTUAL CLARIFICATIONS: This section requires you to define and explain the core terms and issues pertinent to your research topic. Providing clear and concise definitions of the central concepts ensures a shared understanding between you and your readers regarding the fundamental elements of your research. This section can be further subdivided into sub-sub-titles depending on the complexity and number of concepts involved.

THEORETICAL AND HISTORICAL FOUNDATION: Here, you are expected to articulate the jurisprudential basis, theories, and principles that underpin your area of legal study and justify their relevance to your research. Where applicable, this section should also include a brief historical background of your research topic. For instance, research in human rights law would necessitate a discussion of relevant human rights theories and a historical overview of their evolution. This section can also be further broken down into sub-sections.

LITERATURE REVIEW/EMPIRICAL FRAMEWORK: This vital section involves a critical review of existing written or published works by recognized scholars and other authors that relate to your research topic. You should analyze the opinions of authorities and the findings of prior studies in your field. The literature review serves several key purposes:

To demonstrate your familiarity with the existing body of knowledge in your area of research.

To identify any existing gaps, weaknesses, or inconsistencies within the current literature.

To understand how previous research efforts relate to and potentially inform your own study.

To provide a rationale for your research by highlighting how it will contribute a novel perspective, address identified gaps, or strengthen the existing knowledge base.

The NALT guide emphasizes the importance of using credible sources for your literature review, stating that while you can consult journals, books, and online articles, a greater proportion of your reviewed materials should come from peer-reviewed journals. Hard copies of textbooks and reputable online publications are preferred over less reliable online sources. Notably, the NALT guide explicitly discourages the use of Wikipedia as a research source. In the context of non-doctrinal research, this section might also be known as the empirical framework, focusing on the review of previous field or empirical studies.

Structure and Consistency

The NALT manual highlights that all students are expected to structure Chapter Two in a similar manner, regardless of the specific focus of their research topics. This promotes uniformity in academic legal writing and facilitates a more standardized evaluation process.

Applying NALT Citation in Chapter Two

It is crucial that all sources you consult and refer to within Chapter Two are accurately cited using the NALT citation guide's footnote style. Every definition, theoretical concept, historical detail, and piece of existing literature you discuss must be accompanied by a superscript Arabic numeral within the text, which corresponds to a footnote at the bottom of the page providing the complete bibliographic information of the source. Adhering to proper citation practices demonstrates academic integrity and enables readers to easily verify the foundations of your research. Consult Part Three of the NALT guide for comprehensive instructions on citing various legal and academic materials correctly.

By meticulously developing a well-reasoned and comprehensively researched Chapter Two, you will establish a strong intellectual framework for your legal research in Nigeria, providing the necessary context and justification for the subsequent analysis and findings of your study.

---

NALT Citation Guide: Understanding Doctrinal Legal Research in Nigeria

Doctrinal legal research, often considered the bedrock of legal scholarship, plays a crucial role in understanding and shaping the legal landscape in Nigeria. This blog post will serve as a guide to doctrinal legal research in the Nigerian context, drawing insights from the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide for Legal Research Writing in Nigeria (NALT's Blue Book Basic Guide). This guide, developed by the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT), offers a structured approach to legal research writing tailored to the specific needs of legal education and scholarship in Nigeria.

Understanding Doctrinal Legal Research

The NALT guide defines the doctrinal approach as a purely qualitative method that is basically library/online-based for sourcing research materials. It is identified as the traditional method of researching law as it stands in various legal sources such as constitutions, statutes, regulations, conventions, case law (judicial decisions), journals, and books. This approach is also known by various other names, including library-based research, pure theoretical research, legal dogmatic, black letter law research, or ‘arm-chair’ research.

At its core, doctrinal research involves the interpretation, descriptive analysis, and systematization of legal norms or doctrine. Researchers engaged in this approach address or give commentaries on the philosophical questions underpinning the research, such as the nature or characteristics of the law itself. The process entails an expository examination of legal rules from which doctrines are formulated and disseminated. Doctrinal researchers primarily look for available source materials in their research area and examine, appraise, critique, evaluate, analyse, and use this information as a basis for making recommendations for decision-making and law reform. Importantly, this research approach does not rely on empirical statistical analysis and thus employs qualitative research methods.

Structuring Doctrinal Legal Research According to the NALT Guide

The NALT guide provides a uniform format for the standard presentation of research reports, whether doctrinal or non-doctrinal. However, its guidelines specifically address the structuring of research topics under the doctrinal approach. The guide mandates that a research topic under the undergraduate long essay and master’s dissertation is divided into five chapters, while a PhD thesis must be divided into six chapters.

For emphasis, the NALT guide highlights that Chapters One, Two, and Five (or Six in the case of a PhD thesis) are mandatory for all candidates to structure their project topics in the same way to ensure uniformity.

Here’s a typical structure for doctrinal research in NALT’s format:

CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION

Background to the Study

Statement of Problem (Followed by Research Questions)

Aim and Objectives of the Study

Scope and Limitations of the Study

Significance of the Study

Research Methodology (indicating the doctrinal approach)

Chapters Analysis

CHAPTER TWO: CONCEPTUAL, THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS AND LITERATURE REVIEW

Conceptual Framework (Defining key terms)

Theoretical Framework (Explaining jurisprudential basis)

Literature Review (Discussing relevant published works)

The review should highlight how previous studies relate to the current research, how the current study builds upon or departs from them, and the unique perspective the present research brings. The NALT guide encourages the use of peer-reviewed journals, textbooks, and online publications (with caution against unreliable sources like Wikipedia) for literature reviews.

CHAPTER THREE: This chapter typically involves the re-statement of the main research topic or the subject matter of research for thorough examination and critical analysis. It forms a core analytical part of the research. Examples include titles focusing on the legal and institutional frameworks related to the research topic.

CHAPTER FOUR: This chapter could be a continuation of the analysis from Chapter Three, addressing the application and enforcement of the topic, or focusing on the problems and challenges associated with it. The student researcher has some flexibility in the specific content of this chapter, provided it remains logical and aligned with the preceding chapters. Examples include exploring the causes and effects of the researched phenomenon.

CHAPTER FIVE (For Undergraduate and Master's Dissertations): CONCLUSION

Summary of Findings

Recommendations

Contributions to Knowledge

Areas for Further Studies

Conclusion

CHAPTER FIVE (For PhD Thesis): In a PhD thesis, this chapter often involves a continuation of the in-depth analysis, potentially including a critical examination of challenges or a comparative analysis with other jurisdictions.

CHAPTER SIX (For PhD Thesis Only): CONCLUSION

Summary of Findings

Recommendations

Contributions to Knowledge

Areas for Further Studies

Conclusion

The NALT guide emphasizes that while the content of Chapters Three and Four (and Five for PhD) can vary based on the research topic, Chapters One, Two, and the final chapter (Five or Six) are structured the same way by all students at all levels, irrespective of the choice of topic, ensuring a baseline of uniformity.

The Significance of the NALT Guide for Doctrinal Research in Nigeria

The development and adoption of the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide is a significant achievement for legal education in Nigeria. It directly addresses the long-standing need for a uniform approach to legal research writing and citation that is indigenous to Nigeria. Before its ratification, Nigerian law faculties often relied on foreign citation styles like OSCOLA, MLA, and APA, which failed to fully accommodate local issues in legal research writing and lacked a focus on the structuring of comprehensive research projects.

The NALT guide provides a customised standard format and reference guide specifically for legal research writing in Nigeria. By outlining a clear structure for doctrinal research, it aims to address the perennial problems of poor presentations of both undergraduate and postgraduate research projects and the difficulties associated with external examinations due to a lack of uniformity. The guide's emphasis on a standardised chapter breakdown for doctrinal research, particularly the mandatory nature of the introductory, conceptual/theoretical, and concluding chapters, fosters coherence and ease of assessment.

In conclusion, the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide serves as an invaluable resource for conducting and presenting doctrinal legal research in Nigeria. Its structured approach ensures uniformity, enhances clarity, and promotes a more standardized and contextually relevant framework for legal scholarship within the Nigerian legal academic community. By adhering to the principles outlined in this guide, legal researchers in Nigeria can contribute to a more robust and coherent body of indigenous legal knowledge.

NALT Citation Guide: Understanding Doctrinal vs. Non-Doctrinal Legal Research

Welcome to your guide on the differences between the two major acceptable approaches to legal research writing: Doctrinal (Conceptual/Library-Based) and Non-Doctrinal (Empirical/Socio-Legal) research, following the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide for Legal Research Writing in Nigeria (NALT’s Blue Book Basic Guide). This manual is a nationally approved uniform format and citation guide designed for law faculties and legal research institutes in Nigeria. Adhering to its guidelines will ensure your research paper meets the required academic standards within the Nigerian legal education system.

Understanding these approaches is crucial for framing your research and structuring your work effectively.

Doctrinal (Conceptual/Library-Based) Legal Research

The doctrinal approach is the traditional method of researching law. It is purely qualitative and primarily relies on library and online resources for research materials. This approach focuses on analyzing the law as it exists in sources such as:

Constitutions

Statutes and regulations

Conventions (or treaties) and other international agreements

Case law (judicial decisions)

Legal journals and books

Doctrinal research involves the interpretation, descriptive analysis, and systematization of legal norms or doctrine. Researchers using this approach often provide commentaries on the philosophical questions underpinning the law. The process involves looking for available source materials in the research area and then examining, appraising, critiquing, evaluating, and analyzing this information to form a basis for recommendations. Importantly, this approach is not based on empirical statistical analysis and uses qualitative research methods.

Structuring Research Under the Doctrinal Approach:

The NALT guide specifies that under the doctrinal approach, both undergraduate and master's dissertations are divided into five chapters, while a PhD thesis has six chapters. Chapters One, Two, and the final chapter (Five for undergraduate/master's, Six for PhD) have a mandatory structure to ensure uniformity.

Chapter One: Introduction (as discussed in our previous blog post).

Chapter Two: Conceptual, Theoretical Frameworks and Literature Review (also discussed previously).

Chapters Three and Four (and Five for PhD): These chapters contain the main analysis and discussion of the research topic. Students have more discretion in structuring these chapters, focusing on a thorough examination and critical analysis of the subject matter. Chapter Four can often address the application and enforcement of the law and associated challenges. For a PhD, Chapter Five may involve a deeper critical analysis and examination of challenges, potentially including comparative analysis.

Final Chapter (Five for undergraduate/master's, Six for PhD): Conclusion (encompassing summary of findings, recommendations, contributions to knowledge, areas for further studies, and a final conclusion).

Non-Doctrinal (Empirical/Socio-Legal) Legal Research

The non-doctrinal approach is a scientific approach that uses empirical investigation and scientific data collection methods. It involves fieldwork and employs research techniques such as:

Interviews with structured/unstructured questionnaires

Experimental designs with observations

Public opinion surveys and opinion polls

The aim of non-doctrinal research is to generate data that can be empirically analyzed and verified to draw conclusions. This approach can be used to ascertain the desirability of laws or to find measures to address societal problems. The NALT guide acknowledges that law is an interdisciplinary subject and encourages the exploration of both approaches. However, it notes that most law students in Nigeria may not be extensively exposed to the non-doctrinal approach due to the normative nature of law.

Structuring Research Under the Non-Doctrinal Approach:

The NALT guide indicates that non-doctrinal research also typically follows a six-chapter structure, similar to the doctrinal approach, especially at the postgraduate level. However, there are key differences in the content of some chapters.

Chapter One: Introduction (similar to the doctrinal approach but may include a research hypothesis).

Chapter Two: Conceptual and Theoretical Framework & Literature Review (the literature review may be more elaborate and subdivided).

Chapter Three: Research Methodology: This chapter is unique to the non-doctrinal approach and details the data collection methods used, including primary and secondary data collection techniques, research design, population sampling, and instrument reliability.

Chapters Four and Five: Data Analysis, Presentation of Results, and Discussions.

Chapter Six: Conclusion (similar to the final chapter in the doctrinal approach).

Similarities Between Doctrinal and Non-Doctrinal Approaches (as per NALT):

The NALT guide highlights the following similarities:

Both approaches can contain six chapters (especially at the PhD level) with a similar overall structure.

Chapter One has similar features in both approaches.

Chapters One and Six are largely the same, with minor differences.

Chapter Two is devoted to literature review, theoretical, and conceptual frameworks in both, although the non-doctrinal review might be more elaborate.

Choosing an Approach:

The NALT guide recommends that students should stick to the doctrinal approach as it best suits legal research and is more commonly taught. Postgraduate students are encouraged to consider the non-doctrinal approach provided they have the necessary knowledge and exposure, often obtained from social sciences fields. Students wishing to conduct empirical research may need to request a co-supervisor from the faculty of social science.

Understanding these distinctions will help you choose the most appropriate research approach for your long essay and structure it according to the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide, ultimately leading to a well-researched and coherent piece of academic work.

---

NALT Citation Guide: Understanding Non-Doctrinal Legal Research in Nigeria

Non-doctrinal legal research offers a distinct approach to understanding law in Nigeria, moving beyond the interpretation of legal texts to explore the social, economic, and political contexts in which law operates. This blog post will serve as a guide to non-doctrinal legal research in the Nigerian context, drawing insights from the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide for Legal Research Writing in Nigeria (NALT's Blue Book Basic Guide). Developed by the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT), this guide provides frameworks for both doctrinal and non-doctrinal research within the Nigerian legal academic landscape.

Understanding Non-Doctrinal Legal Research (According to NALT)

The NALT guide describes the non-doctrinal approach as the scientific approach to empirical investigation and scientific data collection using scientific techniques for critical analysis and data presentation of an identified research topic. It adopts an empirical approach through fieldwork. This method involves research designs, population sampling, and the use of research techniques such as interviews with structured/unstructured questionnaires, and experimental designs with observations, which may include participation or non-participation. The goal is often to ascertain the desirability or otherwise of certain legal phenomena or to find measures to address societal problems related to law.

Unlike doctrinal research, which is purely qualitative, the non-doctrinal approach often employs quantitative research methods. It seeks to generate data empirically and verify it to draw conclusions. The NALT guide highlights that law, being an interdisciplinary or a multidisciplinary subject, warrants the exploration of both doctrinal and non-doctrinal (empirical) approaches to teaching and research in legal education. It suggests a paradigm shift towards more empirical research in law to address both legal and non-legal/socio-legal issues.

Structuring Non-Doctrinal Legal Research (NALT Guidelines)

The NALT guide provides a specific chapter structure for research adopting the non-doctrinal approach, primarily intended for Master's and PhD candidates. It notes that where a student wishes to adopt both doctrinal and non-doctrinal approaches, they need to consider the slight differences in structuring and presentation.

The non-doctrinal research, according to the NALT guide, typically contains six chapters, with some structural similarities to the doctrinal approach. However, key differences exist, particularly in Chapters Three, Four, and Five.

Here’s a typical structure for non-doctrinal research in NALT’s format:

CHAPTER ONE: INTRODUCTION

Background to the Study

Research Hypothesis (Followed by no more than 5–6 Research Questions)

Purpose of the Study (OBJECTIVES) (Followed by no more than 5–6 Assumptions of the Study)

Scope and Limitations

Significance of the Study

Synopsis of the Chapters

CHAPTER TWO: CONCEPTUAL AND THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK & LITERATURE REVIEW

Conceptual Clarifications (Defining key terms)

Theoretical and Historical Foundation (Explaining jurisprudential and historical basis)

Literature Review (Reviewing previous empirical and theoretical studies)

This review is expected to be more elaborate than in the doctrinal approach and subdivided into subtitles. It should highlight the summary of the review and the gap in knowledge.

CHAPTER THREE: RESEARCH METHODOLOGY

This chapter is unique to empirical research. It details:

Research design

Population and sample size

Sampling techniques

Instruments for data collection (e.g., questionnaire, interview schedule, observation schedule)

Description of the instrument and its development

Validation of the instrument by at least three experts (excluding the supervisor)

Reliability of the instrument testing for consistency

Methods of data analysis

CHAPTER FOUR: DATA PRESENTATION AND ANALYSIS

This chapter presents the data collected through the chosen research methods and analyzes it using appropriate techniques.

CHAPTER FIVE: DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS

This chapter involves a thorough discussion of the results obtained in Chapter Four, relating them back to the research questions and hypothesis.

CHAPTER SIX: CONCLUSION

Summary of Findings

Recommendations (based on findings)

Contribution to Knowledge (indicating specific areas of contribution)

Suggested Areas for Further Studies

Conclusion (conclusive remarks summarizing the whole research)

Key Differences from Doctrinal Research (NALT Perspective)

The NALT guide clearly distinguishes between the structure of doctrinal and non-doctrinal research:

Chapter Three: In non-doctrinal research, this chapter focuses on data collection and research methodology, while in doctrinal research, it is devoted to the main topic of the research.

Chapters Four and Five: In non-doctrinal research, these chapters cover data analysis and presentation of results, and discussions, respectively. In contrast, Chapter Five of a doctrinal research (for Master's) typically contains critical analysis and examination of challenges, possibly including comparative surveys.

Hypothesis and Objectives: Non-doctrinal research explicitly includes research hypotheses and assumptions in Chapter One, which are not typically found in the doctrinal structure as outlined by the NALT guide.

Challenges and Considerations (NALT's View)

The NALT guide acknowledges that legal research in Nigeria is yet to fully develop capacities to teach the in-depths of the social science non-doctrinal approach to legal research writing. There is also the challenge of finding external examiners in the law field to adequately assess students who solely adopt the empirical approach. Therefore, the guide advises academic lawyers and student researchers to tread this line with caution so as not to lose focus on the peculiarities and uniqueness of legal research.

The NALT guide suggests that any student wishing to conduct empirical research may need to make a special request for a co-supervisor from the faculty of social science. It also notes that most law students in Nigeria are not exposed to the non-doctrinal approach due to the normative nature of law.

The Role of the NALT Guide in Promoting Non-Doctrinal Research

Despite the challenges, the NALT guide includes a detailed structure for non-doctrinal research, indicating its recognition of the importance of this approach for a comprehensive understanding of law. By providing clear guidelines on structuring empirical legal research, the NALT aims to:

Encourage postgraduate students to explore both doctrinal and non-doctrinal approaches, provided they have the necessary knowledge.

Offer a framework for faculties to guide students who choose this method.

Potentially foster greater interdisciplinary collaboration between law faculties and social science departments.

Conclusion

The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide acknowledges the significance of non-doctrinal legal research as a vital tool for understanding the interplay between law and society in Nigeria. While highlighting the existing limitations in its widespread adoption within Nigerian legal academia, the guide provides a structured framework for conducting empirical legal research. By outlining the specific chapter requirements and methodological considerations for the non-doctrinal approach, the NALT encourages a more holistic and contextually grounded engagement with legal scholarship in Nigeria, ultimately contributing to a richer and more nuanced understanding of the Nigerian legal landscape.

---

NALT Citation Guide: Writing an Effective Introduction (Chapter One) in Nigeria

Welcome to our guide on crafting a compelling Chapter One – the INTRODUCTION – for legal research in Nigeria, following the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide. This chapter is the cornerstone of your research, providing the initial framework and direction for your entire study, particularly within the context of postgraduate work like master's dissertations and PhD theses.

The Significance of Chapter One: Setting the Stage

The NALT guide emphasizes that Chapter One is highly technical and crucial for your research project at all levels. It lays the foundation upon which the rest of your work will build. For research employing the doctrinal (conceptual/library-based) legal research approach, which is a primary focus of the NALT manual regarding chapter structuring, the Introduction serves to orient the reader and establish the rationale for your study.

Key Components of Chapter One (Doctrinal Approach)

According to the NALT manual, a well-structured Chapter One under the doctrinal approach typically includes the following essential sub-sections:

BACKGROUND TO THE STUDY: This section should provide a concise yet informative overview of the context that has led to your research topic. It involves briefly describing the relevant ideas, variables, historical developments, or contemporary issues that underpin your chosen area of law. You should articulate the motivation and justification for your research.

STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM (Followed by Research Questions): Here, you must clearly and precisely identify the central problem, gap in knowledge, or unsatisfactory situation that your research aims to address. This statement should ideally be supported by existing literature or observations. Following this, you should formulate specific and focused research questions (typically no more than five or six) that your thesis intends to answer. These questions should directly stem from the stated problem and provide a clear direction for your inquiry.

AIM AND OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY: The aim of your study represents the overarching purpose or goal of your research, often stated as a single sentence that reflects the title of your work. The objectives are the specific, measurable steps you will undertake to achieve your aim and answer your research questions. Often, research questions are reformulated as research objectives using transitive verbs.

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY: In this section, you need to clearly define the boundaries of your research (scope) by specifying the particular aspects of the legal problem you will examine, the geographical area, the specific legal frameworks, and the time period under consideration. Additionally, you should acknowledge any potential constraints or limitations that might influence your research process or the generalizability of your findings, such as time, resources, or access to data.

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY: This part elaborates on the importance, benefits, and potential contributions of your research. You should explain why your study is relevant and who stands to benefit from its findings. Consider the potential impact on legal theory, policy, practice, or the addressing of an existing knowledge gap.

RESEARCH METHODOLOGY: This section outlines the systematic approach and specific methods you will employ to conduct your research and answer your research questions. For a doctrinal study, this primarily involves library/online-based research for sourcing legal materials such as statutes, case law, journals, and books. You should briefly indicate the type of legal research methods you will use, such as historical, analytical, descriptive, or comparative analysis. While the NALT guide indicates that literature review is included here for undergraduates, for postgraduate research, a comprehensive literature review typically forms a separate chapter (Chapter Two).

CHAPTERS ANALYSIS: Conclude your introduction with a concise synopsis or outline of your entire research work. Briefly describe the main content and focus of each subsequent chapter, providing the reader with a clear roadmap of your study's structure and flow. For a PhD thesis, this will typically cover all six chapters. For a Master's dissertation, it will cover the five chapters.

Integrating NALT Citation in Chapter One

While Chapter One primarily focuses on setting the context and outlining your research, it is crucial to remember that any sources you refer to within this chapter must be properly cited using the NALT citation guide's footnote style. Any factual claims, background information, or legal references must be accompanied by a superscript Arabic numeral in the text, which corresponds to a footnote at the bottom of the page providing the full bibliographic details of the source. Refer to Part Three of the NALT guide for detailed instructions on how to cite various types of legal and academic materials, including books, journal articles, statutes, and case law.

By meticulously addressing each of these components and adhering to the NALT citation guidelines even in Chapter One, you will establish a strong, credible, and well-structured foundation for your legal research in Nigeria.

---

Always refer to the official NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide for detailed guidance and specific requirements.

This post will explore the origins and development of the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) Uniform Format and Citation Guide, as detailed in the provided sources. Understanding the background to the NALT format provides context for its importance in standardising legal research and writing in Nigeria.

The Need for a Uniform Approach

The Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) recognised a need for a dedicated uniform format and citation guide to address the challenges associated with a lack of consistency in legal research writing. This inconsistency had negative impacts on legal education in Nigeria.

Key issues that led to the development of the NALT guide included:

Lack of uniformity in research writing across different law faculties.

The use of various foreign citation guides such as OSCOLA, MLA and APA, which might not be fully adapted to the Nigerian context.

Difficulties for external examiners in assessing projects with different formatting styles.

A need for a standardised approach to teaching legal research methodology.

Formation of the NALT Guide

The proposal for a uniform research format and citation guide was initially presented at the NALT Conference held at the University of Ilorin in 2013.

The proposal was accepted and consolidated by the Committee of Deans and Directors at Ebonyi State University in January 2014.

The document was ratified at the NALT Conference held at Afe Babalola University (ABUAD) in 2015.

The NALT Uniform Format and Citation guide was a major achievement of the Association since its inception.

Key Features of the NALT Guide

The NALT guide was designed to be comprehensive and user-friendly, catering to both students and academic researchers.

It is based on existing materials on styles of referencing, drawing much insight from foreign systems like MLA, APA, OSCOLA, and Blue Book.

The guide was designed to be structurally logical and wider in scope than other citation guides.

The NALT guide was designed to be indigenous to tertiary institutions for academic research writing in Nigeria.

It adopts a footnote style of referencing similar to OSCOLA, allowing all consulted material to be visible at a glance.

The manual is divided into four major parts, covering preliminary information, research methodologies, citation guidelines, and format for journal articles.

Evolution of the NALT Guide

The NALT guide has undergone several stages of development, reflecting a commitment to improvement and relevance:

The guide was first used for conference papers in 2016 after its ratification.

The first hard copy publication was in 2019 by the NALT Implementation Committee.

The second edition is more robust, with a greater emphasis on localising cases and statutes, while retaining the principles of OSCOLA.

The manual has nearly reached a hundred percent localising of cases and statutes.

The guide was also made available online.

The Role of Key Individuals

Several individuals played crucial roles in the development of the NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide:

Professor Emily Alemika chaired the Implementation Committee.

Professor Chris Ohuruogu facilitated the guide at Ebonyi State University and chaired the LOC at ABUAD.

Professor Yusuf Aboki intervened to save the document from severe criticism.

Late Professor MOU Gasiokwu was prominent in the proposal and formulation of the NALT Format.

Dr. Abdulkarim Kana supported the initiative of publishing the manual as a monograph.

Implementation and Adoption

The NALT format has been adopted partially or in full by some faculties and legal institutes in Nigeria.

The NALT encourages all law faculties and institutes to embrace the manual in its totality.

The guide has been integrated into local settings at both undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

The Association believes that the NALT format is a significant achievement for legal education in Nigeria.

Conclusion

The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide is the result of a collaborative effort to establish a standardised approach to legal research writing in Nigeria. The guide addresses the unique needs of the Nigerian legal community, providing a framework that enhances the quality and consistency of legal scholarship. This manual, which has evolved over time, has been instrumental in shaping legal research and education in the country.

This blog post has covered the key aspects of the background of the NALT format. The next blog post will examine the different categories of the NALT Format and the structuring of research topics.

This post will delve into the different categories of the NALT format and how it guides the structuring of research topics, particularly within the context of legal research in Nigeria. Understanding these categories and structural guidelines is essential for students and academics aiming to produce coherent and well-organised research.

Categories of the NALT Format

The NALT format is designed to accommodate various types of academic writing, primarily focusing on three main categories:

Undergraduate Long Essays: This category outlines the format for research projects required of undergraduate law students.

Master's Dissertations: This category provides guidelines for structuring master's level research projects.

PhD Theses: This category is for the most advanced level of academic research, providing guidelines for doctoral dissertations.

Journal Articles: This category focuses on the structure and format of articles intended for academic publication.

General Guidelines for Research Writing

Before diving into the specifics, the NALT guidelines emphasise some general principles for good research writing:

Ethical Rules: Research must adhere to ethical rules set by the respective university authorities. These include beneficence, informed consent, anonymity, confidentiality, autonomy, justice, and avoiding plagiarism and copyright infringements.

Topic Choice: Students should choose research topics in consultation with lecturers who are versed in the area of research.

Key Principles: Research in law is governed by the principles of knowing and finding the law, reading the law, and applying the law to solve societal problems.

Qualities of Good Research Topics: Topics should be researchable, sufficiently in-depth, timeless, relevant, clear, concise, and non-sentimental, with empirical results.

Structuring Research Topics

The NALT format provides specific guidelines for structuring research topics into chapters, which are crucial for clarity and logical flow. Here’s an overview:

Undergraduate Long Essays

Number of Chapters: The body of the essay is divided into five main chapters.

Page Length: Minimum of 40 pages, maximum of 80 pages.

Font and Spacing: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing, single side of A4 paper.

Abstract: A non-paragraphed abstract of 200-350 words on a single page with single line spacing.

Footnotes: The NALT citation guide for footnotes shall be adopted.

Bibliography: A list of consulted sources should be prepared.

Master's Dissertations

Number of Chapters: The body of the dissertation is divided into five chapters.

Page Length: Minimum of 80 pages, maximum of 150 pages.

Font and Spacing: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing on A4 paper, single side.

Abstract: A non-paragraphed abstract of 400-500 words, single-spaced on one page.

Footnotes: NALT "in-text" footnoting is adopted.

Bibliography: A table of consulted materials should be prepared.

PhD Theses

Number of Chapters: The body of the thesis is divided into six chapters.

Page Length: Minimum of 200 pages, maximum of 400 pages.

Font and Spacing: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing.

Proposal: Prospective students are expected to submit a short proposal (1-2 pages).

Abstract: The manual doesn't specifically note the abstract length for PhD theses.

Footnotes: NALT footnoting is adopted.

Bibliography: A table of consulted materials should be prepared.

Common Elements Across Categories

All categories share certain common elements:

Preliminaries: These include the title page, approval page, publication and compilers page, table of contents, dedication, forewords, acknowledgement, and preface.

Abstract: A concise summary of the research.

Bibliography/Appendices: A list of all consulted materials, and appendices containing supplementary information.

Footnotes: NALT uses footnotes for citations within the text.

Approaches to Legal Research Writing

NALT recognizes two main approaches to legal research writing:

Doctrinal Approach: This is a library-based qualitative approach involving interpretation and analysis of legal norms, cases, statutes, and other legal sources. The chapters under this approach are generally structured as follows:

Chapter One: Introduction

Chapter Two: Conceptual, Theoretical Frameworks, and Literature Review

Chapters Three and Four: Analysis of the main topic, legal frameworks, or related issues

Chapter Five (or Six for PhD): Conclusion, summary of findings, recommendations, and contribution to knowledge.

Non-Doctrinal Approach: This is an empirical, socio-legal approach involving field work, data collection, quantitative analysis, and scientific techniques. The chapters under this approach are structured as follows:

Chapter One: Introduction

Chapter Two: Conceptual, Theoretical Frameworks, and Literature Review

Chapter Three: Research Methodology and Data Collection

Chapters Four and Five: Data Analysis, presentation of results, and discussions

Chapter Six: Conclusion, summary of findings, recommendations, and contribution to knowledge.

Conclusion

The NALT format provides a comprehensive framework for structuring research projects across various academic levels. By understanding the specific requirements for each category and adhering to the provided guidelines, students and academics can produce high-quality, well-organised legal research that meets the standards set by the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers.

This blog post has covered the key aspects of the categories and structuring of research topics under the NALT format. The next blog post will explore the NALT citation guidelines for style of referencing.

blogs.content:
In legal research, primary sources form the bedrock of your arguments and analysis. These sources include statutes, treaties, and case law – the direct outputs of legislative and judicial bodies. The NALT (Nigerian Association of Law Teachers) citation guide provides a clear and consistent method for citing these essential materials. This post will focus on how to accurately cite primary legal sources using the NALT format, providing practical examples to guide you.

What are Primary Sources in Legal Research?

Primary sources in law are the original documents that establish the legal framework. These include:

Statutes (or pieces of legislation): These are laws enacted by a legislative body, such as the National Assembly.

Treaties and Other International Agreements: These are formal agreements between countries or international organisations, which may have legal implications.

Case Law (Judicial Decisions): These are judgments and rulings made by courts, which interpret and apply the law.

Constitutions: These are the fundamental legal principles of a country, and all other laws are subordinate to them.

Using these sources correctly is crucial for the credibility and accuracy of your research. The NALT guide ensures that all primary sources are cited consistently and clearly.

General Rules for Citing Primary Sources

Before delving into specific source types, it's essential to note the general rules within the NALT citation style:

Footnotes: All citations appear as footnotes at the bottom of the page, indicated by a superscript Arabic numeral in the text.

Minimal Punctuation: The NALT guide uses punctuation sparingly. For example, full stops are not used after abbreviations.

Italics: Case names should be in italics, except for the "v" (which replaces "versus") and the first letter of the names.

"v" instead of "versus": The abbreviation "v" is used in place of "versus" or "vs" without a full stop.

Consistency: Cite cases exactly as they appear in the original source. However, for ease of use, round or square brackets can be used consistently, rather than using both.

Citing Specific Primary Sources

Now, let’s explore how to cite each type of primary source using the NALT format:

1. Citing Statutes (or Pieces of Legislation)

When citing a statute, you should include:

The full name of the Act or Law

The Chapter or section number

The year the act was enacted

The abbreviated form of the law

For example:

"Trade Disputes Act, Cap. T8, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004, as updated to 31st December 2010".

Laws of Federation of Nigeria can be abbreviated as LFN instead of L.F.N.

2. Citing Treaties and Other International Agreements

The NALT guide does not provide specific examples on how to cite treaties and other international agreements, but generally, the following details will need to be included:

Full title of the treaty or agreement

Date of signing

Parties to the agreement

Citation information or reference number

3. Citing Case Law (Judicial Decisions)

Citing cases requires careful attention to detail. Here’s how to cite a case using NALT:

Case Names: The names of the parties should be in italics, with an unpunctuated italic "v" separating them.

Year: The year the case was reported should be in square brackets [ ].

Volume and Part: Include the volume number and part number of the law report in brackets ( ).

Page Number: Include the page number or range of pages.

Here are some examples of citing cases:

Okoye v Lagos State Govt. \ 3 NWLR (Pt 136) 115.

IGP v Adedeji \ WRNLR 178.

Abacha v Fawehinmi \ FWLR (Pt 4) 533.

Ezenkwanko v The State \ 2 NWLR (Pt 1443) 265.

Note: Where a law report does not have the style of citation shown above, use the citation provided in that law report.

Using "Re" and "Ex parte"

Re: Use "Re" in preference to "In re" or "In the matter of". For example, use Re the Companies Act 2004.

Ex parte: Abbreviate "Ex parte" (on behalf of) to "Ex p" with a capital "E" only if it is the first word of the case name, and no full stop after "p".

Electronic Law Reports

Cite a case reported electronically (e.g., from Law Pavilion) as indicated on the report itself, possibly including the website.

There is a recognised order of authority in case reporting, with the abbreviated form always given.

Some law reports to know include: Supreme Court of Nigeria Judgments (SCNJ); Nigerian Supreme Court Quarterly Law Reports (NSCQR); Nigerian Investments and Securities Law Reports (NISLR); Weekly Law Reports (WLR); Law Reports of Courts of Nigeria (LRCN); Nigerian Weekly Law Report (NWLR); and Economic Crimes Law Report (ECLR).

4. Citing the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria

When citing the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999:

In the first instance, it should be cited in full, with the word "as amended" attached to it.

Practical Application

Let’s look at a few examples of how to use this in practice. Suppose you are discussing a case in your research paper, you would write something like:

"In the case of Okoye v Lagos State Govt., it was held that..." and then in the footnote you would write:

Okoye v Lagos State Govt. \ 3 NWLR (Pt 136) 115.

This way, your reader can easily locate the source of your information at the bottom of the page.

Conclusion

Correctly citing primary sources is essential for robust legal research. The NALT citation style offers a systematic way to present statutes, treaties, and case law within your work. By adhering to the guidelines outlined above, you can ensure the credibility and accuracy of your legal writing. This post has provided a solid foundation, and the next blog post will focus on citing secondary sources.
