blogs.content:
In legal research, while primary sources such as statutes and case law form the foundation, secondary sources provide the critical analysis, context, and scholarly discourse needed to support your arguments. The NALT (Nigerian Association of Law Teachers) citation guide offers a comprehensive system for citing these sources, ensuring your research is both credible and well-supported. This post will focus on effectively citing secondary sources using the NALT format.

What are Secondary Sources in Legal Research?

Secondary sources are materials that analyse, interpret, or comment on primary legal sources. They provide valuable insights and perspectives that can enhance your understanding of the law. These sources include:

Textbooks: Comprehensive scholarly works on specific areas of law.

Monographs: Detailed studies on a particular legal topic.

Government publications: Documents published by government bodies.

Articles in peer-reviewed journals: Scholarly articles presenting original research and analysis.

Case reviews: Analyses of court decisions.

Periodicals and dailies: Newspapers and magazines.

Edited works: Collections of articles or chapters by different authors, compiled by an editor.

Projects, theses, and dissertations: Academic research papers.

Online sources: Materials published on the internet.

Inaugural and distinguished lectures: Public addresses by legal scholars.

General Rules for Citing Secondary Sources

Before delving into specific source types, it's important to remember the general rules for NALT citations:

Footnotes: Citations appear as footnotes at the bottom of the page, indicated by a superscript Arabic numeral in the text.

Minimal Punctuation: The NALT guide uses punctuation sparingly, avoiding full stops after abbreviations.

Commas: Commas are used to separate the name of the author/co-authors from the title of the work.

Colons: A colon is used to separate a title from a subtitle.

Italics: Titles of books and journals are italicised.

Single quotation marks: Titles of articles in journals, newspapers, magazines, chapters in books etc., should be in single quotation marks.

Cross-Referencing: The Latin expressions like supra, infra, ante, and op cit are not used in the NALT style guide, but ibid is used, and cross-references are used with [n] to indicate the footnote where a source was first cited.

Citing Specific Secondary Sources

Now, let's look at how to cite each type of secondary source using the NALT format:

1. Citing Textbooks

When citing a book, include the following:

Author's name: Exactly as it appears in the publication, omitting prefixes or titles like Mr., Mrs., Dr., etc..

Title of the book: In italics.

Edition (if applicable): In brackets.

Publisher: In brackets.

Year of publication: In brackets.

Here are some examples:

Bethel Uzoma Ihugba, Introduction to Legal Research Method and Legal Writing (Malthouse Press, 2020).

A Okoh Alubo, Criminal Procedure Law in Nigeria (Innovative Communications 2012).

Muhammed Tawfiq Ladan, Sustainable Development Goals, Climate Change and Extractive Resource Management in Africa (Ahmadu Bello University Press Limited Zaria 2017).

Martin U Gasiokwu, Legal Research and Methodology: The A-Z of Writing Theses and Dissertations in a Nutshell.

Books with Multiple Authors

Two or three authors: Include all names, separated by "and". Example: D Chalmers and G Davies and G Monti, European Union Law: Text and Materials (2nd edn, CU Publication 2010).

More than three authors: Give the first author's details and add "and others". Example: CA Omaka and others, Municipal and International Environmental Law (LUC Publishers Lagos, 2012).

Edited books: When citing a chapter in a book edited by one or more people, cite the author and title of the contribution, followed by the editor's name(s) using "ed" or "eds", the title of the book, and the publication information. Example: David Jangkam, "The Value of Authorship in the Digital Environment" in Clement Francis Kwede and Karen Shaakaa (eds), World Wide Research: Reshaping the Sciences and Humanities in the Century of Information (MIT, 2010), 62-80.

2. Citing Monographs, Lecture Notes, and Conference Papers

Monographs: Cited like textbooks.

Lecture notes: Include the author’s name, the title of the material (as for a book), the nature of the document, and the date. Example: Patrick Ndubisi Oche, A Critique of the Petroleum Industry Bill (A Lecture Note prepared for graduate students and final year undergraduate students of the Faculty of Law, University of Jos 2015).

Conference papers: Include the author’s name, the title of the paper in single quotation marks, the occasion, place, and date of presentation (in brackets) and the page number(s). Example: Alphonsus I Alubo and others, "Plea Bargain Mechanism in the Judicial Determination of Corruption Cases: A Critical Inter-Jurisdictional Assessment" (a conference proceedings of the 46th annual conference of the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers, held at the Auditorium and Faculty of Law, University of Ilorin from 22nd to 26th April 2013) 235-271.

3. Citing Articles in Journals

For journal articles, include:

Author's name: As it appears in the publication.

Title of the article: In single quotation marks.

Name of the journal: In italics or its abbreviation.

Year of publication: In square or round brackets.

Volume and issue number: In brackets, if any.

Page number(s): Where necessary.

Examples:

EI Alemika, "Criminal Justice System and Respect for Human Rights: Problems and Imperatives for Reform" Human Rights Review: An International Human Rights Journal (l2) (2) 25.

A Okoh Alubo and Dominic Asada, "A Critical Examination of Offences Antecedent to and in the Course of Winding up of Companies under Nigerian Law" Current Jos Law Journal 5 (5) 210.

4. Citing Online Journals

If an article is published electronically, follow the guidelines for hard copy journals and include:

The web address in angle brackets <>.

The date of the most recent access.

Example: CJ Dakas, "The Right of Franchise and the Imperative of a Credible Electoral System in Nigeria" EJLT (2010) 1(1) http://ejlt.org/article/view/17 accessed 27 July 2010.

5. Citing Periodicals/Dailies (Newspapers/Magazines)

Include:

Author's name: As it appears in the publication.

Title of the article: In single quotation marks.

Name of the newspaper: In italics.

City of publication: In brackets.

Date of publication.

Page number(s): Where necessary.

Example: JN Aduba, "Constitutionalism and Citizenship: What is the Way Forward!" New Era Magazine (Lagos, 13 October 2012) 10.

If the item is an editorial, cite "Editorial" as the author.

6. Citing Projects, Master's Dissertations, and PhD Theses

Cite these as you would a book, including the author's name, the title of the work, and the type of document, and the institution, and year the document was submitted.

Example: Matthias Zechariah, Genocide under International Criminal Law: Past, Present and Future Concerns in Africa (LLM Dissertation Faculty of Law University of Jos 2011).

7. Citing Inaugural Lectures and Distinguished Lecture Series

Include the title (in italics), the occasion, place, and date of presentation in brackets.

Example: Dakas CJ From Constitutions to Constitutionalism: A Constitutional Imperative in Nigeria (Being the Ben Nwabueze Distinguished Professor of Law Lecture presented in Abuja, Nigeria on 18th November 2013).

Practical Application

Let's see how this works in practice. Suppose you want to cite a journal article by E.I Alemika:

You would write in your text: "Alemika has argued that..." and then, in the footnote, you would write:

EI Alemika, "Criminal Justice System and Respect for Human Rights: Problems and Imperatives for Reform" Human Rights Review: An International Human Rights Journal (l2) (2) 25.

Bibliography

The bibliography should be a comprehensive list of all sources cited in your work, formatted according to the NALT style. Here are some key points:

Surname First: List entries by the author's surname, followed by their initials, then a comma. For example, Ogboru TO.

No page numbers: Generally, page numbers are not provided in bibliography entries for journal articles.

Alphabetical Order: Entries should be listed alphabetically by the author's surname.

Initials: Only initials of forenames should be used, not full forenames.

Unattributed Works: List unattributed works at the beginning of the bibliography, in alphabetical order of the first major word of the title.

Multiple Works by the Same Author: List multiple works by the same author in chronological order, starting with the oldest.

Co-Authored Works: If the first author has more than one co-authored work, list them alphabetically by the co-author's surname.

Conclusion

Mastering the citation of secondary sources is vital for producing high-quality legal research. The NALT citation style, with its detailed guidelines and consistent approach, provides a solid framework for presenting your work effectively. This guide should equip you with the tools to confidently cite a variety of secondary sources in your academic and professional writing, thereby enhancing the overall quality and credibility of your research. The next blog post will focus on the structure of legal research papers using the NALT format.

Accurate citation of books, journals, and articles is a fundamental aspect of legal research. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides specific rules for referencing these sources, ensuring clarity and consistency in Nigerian legal scholarship. This guide will walk you through the correct way to cite books, journals, and articles using NALT formatting.

1. Citing Books in NALT Format

A book citation in NALT format follows this structure:

Author’s Name, Title (Edition, Publisher Year) Page.

Example:

A. Oluwole, Nigerian Constitutional Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021) 67.

B. Adekunle, Judicial Review in Nigeria (1st edn, Lagos Law Press 2019) 120.

Key Rules:

The author’s name appears in the order of first initial, followed by the surname in footnotes.

The title of the book is italicised.

The edition (if applicable) is indicated in parentheses.

The publisher and year of publication follow the edition.

The specific page referenced is indicated at the end.

2. Citing Journal Articles in NALT Format

For journal articles, the citation includes the article title, journal title, volume, issue, year, and page number.

Author’s Name, ‘Title of Article’ (Year) Volume(Issue) Journal Name Page.

Example:

O. Adeyemi, ‘Human Rights in Nigerian Courts’ (2020) 14(2) Nigerian Journal of Legal Studies 45.

T. Bello, ‘Corporate Governance in Africa’ (2019) 10(1) African Business Law Review 78.

Key Rules:

The author’s name follows the same order as books (initial, then surname).

The article title appears in single quotation marks.

The year of publication is placed in parentheses.

The journal title is italicised.

The volume number appears before the issue number (if applicable).

The page number refers to where the article starts.

3. Citing Chapters in Edited Books

When citing a specific chapter within an edited book, the citation follows this format:

Author’s Name, ‘Title of Chapter’ in Editor’s Name (ed), Title (Publisher Year) Page.

Example:

F. Ojo, ‘Legal Pluralism in Nigeria’ in A. Bamidele (ed), African Legal Systems (Cambridge University Press 2018) 90.

Key Rules:

The chapter author’s name appears first.

The chapter title is in single quotation marks.

The editor’s name follows with ‘(ed)’ to indicate editorship.

The book title is italicised.

The publisher and year appear after the title.

The page number of the chapter is specified at the end.

4. Citing Online Articles

With digital sources becoming more common, it is essential to cite online articles correctly. The format includes the URL and access date.

Author’s Name, ‘Title’ (Date) Website Name accessed [Day Month Year].

Example:

M. Ajayi, ‘AI and the Future of Nigerian Law’ (10 March 2022) TechLaw Nigeria https://www.techlawng.com/ai-law accessed 5 June 2022.

Key Rules:

The author’s name follows standard format.

The article title is in single quotation marks.

The date of publication is included (if available).

The website name is italicised.

The URL is enclosed in angle brackets.

The access date is included at the end.

5. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Forgetting italics – Book and journal titles must always be italicised.

Omitting page numbers – Always include a specific page reference when necessary.

Incorrect order of citation elements – Ensure all elements appear in the correct sequence.

Using ‘et al.’ incorrectly – For books or articles with multiple authors, list up to three authors; use et al. only for four or more authors.

6. Using the NALT Citation Generator for Books and Articles

To simplify your citations, use the NALT Citation Generator available on our website. Simply enter the details, and the tool will generate properly formatted citations instantly.

Conclusion

Correctly citing books, journals, and articles is essential for legal research and academic writing. The NALT Format ensures uniformity, professionalism, and clarity. By following these guidelines, you can maintain high citation standards in your legal work.

blogs.content:
Citing legislation and government documents correctly is crucial in legal research. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides a structured approach to referencing these sources, ensuring clarity and uniformity in Nigerian legal writing. This guide explains how to cite legislation and government documents following the NALT format.

1. Citing Nigerian Legislation

A typical citation for Nigerian legislation follows this format:

Title of Legislation Year, Section (if applicable).

Example:

Electoral Act 2022, s 10.

Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, ss 45–47.

Evidence Act 2011, pt IV.

Key Rules:

The title of the legislation is written in full without italics.

The year of enactment follows immediately after the title.

Specific sections, subsections, or parts are indicated using abbreviations (e.g., s for section, pt for part).

2. Citing Subsidiary Legislation

When citing subsidiary legislation (e.g., regulations, rules, or orders), follow this structure:

Title of Subsidiary Legislation (made under Name of Principal Act) Year.

Example:

Companies Regulations (made under the Companies and Allied Matters Act) 2021.

Legal Practitioners (Disciplinary Committee) Rules (made under the Legal Practitioners Act) 2007.

3. Citing Nigerian Constitutional Provisions

When citing the Nigerian Constitution, use the following structure:

Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria Year, Article or Section.

Example:

Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, s 36(1).

Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), art 12.

4. Citing Government Reports and Official Documents

For government reports, policy papers, and other official documents, use this format:

Government Body, Title (Publisher Year) Page.

Example:

Federal Ministry of Justice, White Paper on Judicial Reforms (Government Press 2021) 15.

National Assembly, Committee Report on Electoral Reforms (Lagos Printing Press 2019) 78.

Key Rules:

The issuing government body is listed first.

The title of the document is italicised.

The publisher and year appear after the title.

If citing a specific page, include it at the end.

5. Citing International Treaties and Conventions

For treaties and conventions ratified by Nigeria, use this format:

Title, Date, Treaty Series (if applicable).

Example:

African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights 1981, OAU Doc CAB/LEG/67/3 rev 5.

United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989, 1577 UNTS 3.

Key Rules:

The title of the treaty or convention is written in full.

The year of adoption is included.

If available, include the treaty series citation (e.g., UNTS, OAU Doc).

6. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Incorrect abbreviation of sections and parts – Always use ‘s’ for section, ‘ss’ for multiple sections, and ‘pt’ for part.

Failing to italicise official reports – Government reports and white papers should be italicised.

Omitting the year of legislation – Always include the year to differentiate between versions of an act.

Confusing subsidiary legislation with principal acts – Ensure subsidiary legislation references its parent act.

Conclusion

Citing legislation and government documents accurately ensures compliance with legal research standards. By following the NALT Format, researchers, students, and practitioners can maintain consistency and professionalism in legal writing.

blogs.content:
Legal research and writing require precise and consistent citation of sources, particularly court cases. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides a standardised approach for citing Nigerian case law, ensuring clarity, uniformity, and compliance with legal research standards in Nigeria. This guide will walk you through the process of citing Nigerian cases using the NALT citation style.

1. Understanding the NALT Citation Format for Cases

The NALT format for citing cases follows a structure similar to OSCOLA but is tailored to Nigerian legal practice. The basic format includes:

Case Name [Year] Volume (if available) Report Series Abbreviation Page.

Example:

Adeyemi v State [2018] 10 NWLR (Pt. 1635) 23.

In this format:

Adeyemi v State → The case name (italicised)

[2018] → The year of the case (placed in square brackets if the year is essential for finding the case, or in round brackets if not)

10 NWLR → The volume of the Nigerian Weekly Law Reports

(Pt. 1635) → The part number of the law report

23 → The first page of the report where the case starts

2. Citing Unreported Cases

For unreported judgments, NALT requires the following elements:

Case Name (Suit No, Court, Date of Judgment, Unreported).

Example:

Olawale v FRN (Suit No SC/234/2022, Supreme Court, 15 June 2022, Unreported).

If a case is unreported, it should be explicitly stated as “Unreported” at the end.

3. Citing Cases with Multiple Parties

When there are multiple parties in a case, only the first claimant and the first defendant are cited. If the parties are government institutions, abbreviations may be used where appropriate.

Example:

Nigeria Customs Service v Johnson [2020] 5 SCNJ 78.

For government cases:

Attorney-General of Lagos State v Attorney-General of the Federation [2015] 6 NWLR (Pt. 1456) 1.

4. Using Citation Signals

In legal writing, citation signals help clarify how the cited case supports or contradicts an argument. The NALT format recognises standard citation signals such as:

See – Used when the case directly supports the argument.

Cf. – Used when the case provides a contrasting but relevant point.

See also – Used when additional cases further reinforce the argument.

Example in Footnotes:

See Adeyemi v State [2018] 10 NWLR (Pt. 1635) 23.

5. Comparing NALT with OSCOLA for Nigerian Cases

While OSCOLA (Oxford University Standard for the Citation of Legal Authorities) is widely used in international legal research, it does not fully align with Nigerian legal referencing. The key differences include:

Feature

NALT Citation

OSCOLA Citation

Case Name

Italicised

Italicised

Year Format

[Year] in square brackets if essential, (Year) in round brackets otherwise

[Year] always in square brackets

Abbreviations

Nigerian law reports only

British and international reports

Unreported Cases

Includes suit number, court, and date

Often includes a neutral citation

6. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Failing to italicise case names – All case names must be italicised.

Incorrectly formatting unreported cases – Always include the suit number, court, and date.

Using OSCOLA instead of NALT – Nigerian legal research requires adherence to NALT guidelines.

Omitting citation signals – These are crucial for legal arguments.

7. Using the NALT Citation Generator for Case Citations

To simplify the citation process, you can use the NALT Citation Generator on our website. Just enter the case details, and the tool will generate a properly formatted citation instantly.

Conclusion

Proper citation of Nigerian case law is essential for academic and professional legal writing. The NALT Citation Guide provides a standardised approach that aligns with Nigerian legal scholarship. By following these guidelines, law students, researchers, and practitioners can ensure their work meets the highest standards of accuracy and professionalism.

For more resources and automated citation tools, visit our NALT Citation Generator page!

blogs.content:
Proper citation is crucial in legal writing, ensuring clarity, consistency, and academic integrity. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides a structured approach to formatting footnotes and bibliographies in Nigerian legal research. This guide will help you master the essentials of NALT-style citations for footnotes and bibliographies.

1. Understanding NALT Footnote Formatting

NALT adopts a footnote citation style, similar to OSCOLA, ensuring that all references appear at the bottom of each page rather than within the main text.

Basic Footnote Format

A standard footnote follows this structure:

Author Name, Title (Edition, Publisher Year) Page.

Example:

A. Oluwole, Principles of Nigerian Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021) 45.

Citing Cases in Footnotes

Case citations in footnotes follow this format:

Adeyemi v State [2018] 10 NWLR (Pt. 1635) 23.

Citing Legislation

Legislation is cited without italics and follows this structure:

Electoral Act 2022, s 10.

For multiple references within a footnote, separate citations with a semicolon:

Olawale v FRN (Suit No SC/234/2022, Supreme Court, 15 June 2022, Unreported); Electoral Act 2022, s 15.

2. Cross-Referencing and Shortened Citations

To avoid redundancy, subsequent citations can be shortened using ‘ibid’ or a short form:

Using 'Ibid'

If the same source is cited consecutively, use ibid.

A. Oluwole, Principles of Nigerian Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021) 45.

Ibid 48.

Shortened Form for Later Citations

For non-consecutive references, use the author’s surname and a shortened title:

A. Oluwole, Principles of Nigerian Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021) 45.

Oluwole, Principles, 67.

3. Formatting Bibliographies in NALT Style

A bibliography appears at the end of the document and provides a full list of sources consulted. Unlike footnotes, entries are structured differently:

Authors are listed surname first.

Entries are not numbered.

Sources are grouped under Primary Sources (Cases, Legislation) and Secondary Sources (Books, Articles).

Example Bibliography Format

Primary Sources

Adeyemi v State [2018] 10 NWLR (Pt. 1635) 23.

Electoral Act 2022.

Secondary Sources

Oluwole A, Principles of Nigerian Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021).

Adekunle T, ‘Judicial Review in Nigerian Law’ (2020) 14(2) Nigerian Journal of Legal Studies 56.

4. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Omitting italics for case names – All case names must be italicised.

Failing to list authors by surname first in the bibliography – Unlike footnotes, bibliographies list authors by surname first.

Incorrect use of ‘ibid’ – Only use ibid when the previous citation is identical.

Using punctuation incorrectly – Ensure commas, full stops, and colons are correctly placed.

5. Using the NALT Citation Generator for Footnotes and Bibliographies

To simplify citation formatting, use the NALT Citation Generator on our website. Simply input your sources, and it will generate correctly formatted footnotes and bibliography entries.

Conclusion

Mastering NALT-style footnotes and bibliographies is essential for legal research and academic writing in Nigeria. By following these guidelines, you ensure clarity, professionalism, and adherence to Nigerian legal citation standards.

blogs.author: NALT Cite Editorial Team
blogs.excerpt: Proper formatting of quotations, punctuation, and italics is essential for clarity and consistency in legal writing. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides specific rules for handling ...
blogs.content:
Proper formatting of quotations, punctuation, and italics is essential for clarity and consistency in legal writing. The NALT Uniform Format and Citation Guide provides specific rules for handling these elements in citations and references. This guide explains how to apply quotation marks, punctuation, and italics correctly when using NALT referencing.

1. Using Quotation Marks in NALT Referencing

Quotation marks are used to indicate direct quotes and short article titles.

Short Quotations (Less than Three Lines)

Short quotations should be enclosed in double quotation marks and incorporated into the text.

Example: According to Justice Adeyemi, “Judicial independence is a cornerstone of democracy.”

Place punctuation outside the closing quotation mark unless it is part of the original quote.

Example: Justice Okonkwo argued, “A fair trial is fundamental to justice”.

Long Quotations (Three or More Lines)

Long quotations should be indented, single-spaced, and without quotation marks.

Example:

Justice Adeyemi stated:

The principle of separation of powers is essential in preventing the abuse

of authority and ensuring accountability within a democratic system.

2. Punctuation in Legal Citations

Proper punctuation ensures that citations remain clear and readable.

Basic Punctuation Rules:

Use commas to separate elements within citations.

Place full stops at the end of footnotes and bibliographic entries.

Use colons to separate volumes and page numbers in journal citations.

Examples:

A. Oluwole, Principles of Nigerian Law (2nd edn, Oxford University Press 2021) 45.

O. Adeyemi, ‘Human Rights in Nigerian Courts’ (2020) 14(2) Nigerian Journal of Legal Studies 45.

3. Italics in NALT Referencing

Italics are used for specific elements to enhance readability and maintain consistency.

When to Use Italics:

Case Names – Always italicise case names.

Example: Adeyemi v State [2018] 10 NWLR (Pt. 1635) 23.

Book and Journal Titles – Italicise the titles of books and law journals.

Example: A. Oluwole, Nigerian Constitutional Law (Oxford University Press 2021).

Foreign Words or Phrases – If commonly used in English, do not italicise.

Example: Bona fide, inter alia, res judicata.

What Not to Italicise:

Legislation Titles – Do not italicise Nigerian statutes.

Example: Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, s 10.

Quotation Marks Within Quotations – Use single quotation marks for quotations within another quotation.

Example: According to Justice Adeyemi, “The court ruled that ‘every accused person is entitled to legal representation’ in all circumstances.”

4. Common Mistakes to Avoid

Misplacing punctuation with quotations – Ensure punctuation is placed correctly.

Failing to italicise case names and book titles – Always italicise these elements.

Using italics for legislation – Nigerian laws should not be italicised.

Overusing italics – Reserve italics for necessary elements only.

5. Using the NALT Citation Generator for Formatting

For accuracy and consistency, use the NALT Citation Generator on our website. It automatically formats citations with correct punctuation, italics, and quotation marks.

Conclusion

Mastering the correct use of quotation marks, punctuation, and italics is essential for legal research and writing. By following NALT guidelines, you ensure clarity, professionalism, and adherence to Nigerian legal citation standards.

For more tools and resources, visit our NALT Citation Generator today!

blogs.author: NALT Cite Editorial Team

blogs.content:
This post will explore the specific formatting requirements for articles intended for publication in academic journals, as outlined by the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT). This is a crucial aspect of legal scholarship, ensuring that research is presented clearly, consistently, and professionally.

Key Features of Journal Articles

NALT guidelines specify that journal articles possess certain characteristics:

They are on very specific topics.

They are shorter than books.

They are generally written by researchers or scholars for a department or faculty.

They use scholarly or technical language.

They tend to be long and detailed.

They are about research in a particular academic discipline.

They include full citations for all sources.

They are often peer-reviewed.

They include information about the authors.

They are mostly published by academic organisations.

Structure of Journal Articles

According to the NALT guidelines, articles should include the following elements in a logical order:

Introduction: This should introduce the topic, its importance and relevance.

Body: The main body of the article will typically include several sections, such as a historical background, theoretical framework, conceptual clarification, and an analysis of key elements.

Conclusion/Recommendations: This is where the author summarises findings and provides recommendations.

Sub-Main Titles and Sub-Sub Titles

Sub-main titles are in capital letters and aligned to the left margin, with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3 etc.).

Sub-sub-titles are in small letters, with the first letter of each word capitalised, except for words such as 'of', 'and', 'or', and 'the'. There is no limit to the number of sub-sub titles. Sub-subtitles may be numbered in Roman numerals (i, ii, iii, etc.) or in alphabetical order (a, b, c, etc.).

NALT Guide for Contributors

NALT also provides a style guide for contributors to journals:

The title of the article should be concise and capture the essence of the work.

An abstract of not more than 250 words should be included, summarising the key findings and arguments.

Keywords should be provided to aid indexing and searchability.

The main body of the text must use Times New Roman font, size 12, and double line spacing.

Margins should be 1 inch (2.54 cm) on all sides.

Page numbers should be at the centre of the bottom of the page.

Spelling should adhere to British English.

Sources should be cited using footnotes in Times New Roman font size 10, indicated in the text with superscript Arabic numerals.

Articles that do not conform to these guidelines will not be considered for publication.

Referencing Style in Articles

The NALT referencing style uses footnotes and is similar to OSCOLA. NALT uses punctuation minimally.

Books: Give the author's name as it appears in the publication, omitting prefixes and titles. The title should be in italics, and the publication information in brackets.

Multiple Authors: For up to three authors, insert 'and' between their names. For more than three authors, give details of the first author and add 'and others'.

Chapters in Books: Cite the author of the chapter, the chapter title in single quotation marks, followed by the book editors, the book title in italics, and publication information.

Journals: Include the author's name, the title of the article in single quotation marks, the name of the journal in italics, the year of publication, volume number and issue number in brackets, and page numbers.

Conference Proceedings: Cite the author, the title of the paper, and the conference details, including the year.

Newspapers and Magazines: Include the author, title of the article, name of the publication in italics, and the date.

Online Journals: Include the author, the title of the article, the name of the journal in italics, and the year of publication, followed by the web address in angle brackets and the date accessed.

Cases: Case names should be in italics with an unpunctuated "v" between the names. Provide the year of the report, the volume number, and the part number and page number. Subsequent citations of the same case can be in a shortened form.

Specimens for Footnotes

NALT guidelines give specific examples for citing different types of materials:

Book: Usman M Shuaib, Legal Issues and Shari’ah Governance on Islamic Banking in Nigeria (Benchmark Publishers 2018). In the bibliography, this would be cited as: Shuaib, UM, Legal Issues and Shari’ah Governance on Islamic Banking in Nigeria

Journal: Friday Nwoke, "International Labour Law: An Appraisal" Journal of Public Law and Constitutional Practice (2005) 3(1) 40-51.

Conference Proceedings: A Omakwu and I Ifekapdu, "Towards Effective AU-REC Regional Regime in West Africa: An Examination of the Role of GIABA in Law and Economy" Nigerian Law Teachers (NALT) Conference Proceedings (2016) 812-820.

Newspaper: Ogbonna Elekwa, "Economic Growth in Nigeria" This Day Weekly Magazine 5 Feb 2015.

Case Review: Amaka Ajunwa, "Passing Off in Cases of Image Rights and False Merchandising in Nigeria (Fenty v Artecoco)" Nigerian Current Legal Problems (NIALS Journal) (2016-2017) 9&10.

Online Journal: Clement Dakas, "The Right of Franchise and the Imperative of a Credible Electoral System in Nigeria" EJLT (2010) 1(1) http://ejlt.org/article/view/17 accessed 27 July 2010.

Conclusion

The NALT guidelines for structuring articles for journal publication provide a clear pathway for legal scholars in Nigeria. By adhering to these formatting and citation rules, authors can ensure that their research is presented professionally and is easily accessible to the wider legal community. These guidelines, when followed, enhance the quality and credibility of legal scholarship in Nigeria and beyond.

This blog post has covered the key aspects of the NALT format for articles in journals. The next blog post will delve into the history of the formation of the NALT uniform format and citation guide.

blogs.title: Structuring Legal Research Papers with NALT
blogs.author: NALT Cite Editorial Team
blogs.excerpt: The Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) provides a detailed framework for structuring legal research papers, ensuring clarity, coherence, and consistency in academic legal writing. This pos...
blogs.content:
The Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) provides a detailed framework for structuring legal research papers, ensuring clarity, coherence, and consistency in academic legal writing. This post will focus on how to effectively structure different types of legal research papers, such as undergraduate essays, master's dissertations, and PhD theses, using the NALT format.

General Principles of NALT Structure

The NALT format emphasizes a logical and systematic approach to research writing. Key principles include:

Uniformity: The format aims to achieve uniformity across Nigerian law faculties and research institutes.

Logical Order: Research topics should be broken down into chapters and sub-sections in a logical manner.

Mandatory Chapters: Certain chapters (such as the introduction and conclusion) have a mandatory structure, promoting consistency.

Flexibility: While maintaining a standard structure, the NALT format also allows some flexibility for students to develop their arguments.

Footnotes: The NALT format uses footnotes for citations and additional explanations.

Categories of Research Papers

The NALT guide categorizes research papers into three main types:

Undergraduate long essays

Master's dissertations

PhD theses

Each category has specific requirements regarding the number of chapters, page limits, and other formatting details.

Structuring Undergraduate Long Essays

An undergraduate long essay, according to NALT guidelines, should include the following:

Five Main Chapters: The body of the essay should be divided into five main chapters.

Preliminaries: The chapters are preceded by preliminaries.

Bibliography and Appendices: The chapters are followed by a bibliography and appendices (if any).

Page Length: The essay should be between 40 and 80 pages.

Font: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing, and one side of the paper should be used for typing.

Abstract: A non-paragraphed abstract of one page with 200-350 words.

Chapter Titles: Each chapter must have a title in capital letters. Subtitles should be assigned a number in Arabic numerals while sub-sub-titles are assigned a sub-Arabic numeral.

Footnotes: NALT citation guide should be used for footnotes within the text.

Bibliography: Students should also prepare a list of consulted sources.

Structuring Master's Dissertations

A Master's dissertation should be structured as follows:

Five Main Chapters: The body of the dissertation is divided into five chapters.

Preliminaries: The chapters are preceded by preliminaries.

Bibliography and Appendices: The chapters are followed by a bibliography and appendices (if any).

Page Length: The dissertation should be between 80 and 150 pages.

Font: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing, on A4 paper, and one side of the paper should be used for typing.

Abstract: A non-paragraphed abstract of one page with 400-500 words.

Footnotes: NALT footnotes are to be adopted in-text.

Bibliography: Students are also expected to prepare a table of bibliography of consulted materials.

Oral Examination: Students are expected to undergo an oral examination to defend their work.

Structuring PhD Theses

A PhD thesis has a more extensive structure:

Six Main Chapters: The thesis is divided into six main chapters.

Preliminaries: The chapters are preceded by preliminaries.

Bibliography and Appendices: The chapters are followed by a bibliography and appendices (if any).

Page Length: The thesis should be between 200 and 400 pages.

Font: Times New Roman, font size 12, double spacing, on A4 paper, and one side of the paper should be used for typing.

Proposal: Prospective students are expected to write and submit a short proposal.

Abstract: A non-paragraphed abstract is included with 500-600 words.

Footnotes: The NALT citation guide is used for footnotes within the text.

Bibliography: Students are also expected to prepare a list of consulted sources.

Oral Defense: Candidates are expected to present a final defense (viva voce) after an internal defense.

Detailed Chapter Structure

The NALT format prescribes specific content for certain chapters, particularly under the doctrinal approach.

Doctrinal Approach

Under the doctrinal approach, the following chapter structure is typical:

Chapter One: Introduction:

Background to the study.

Statement of the problem.

Aim and objectives of the study.

Scope and limitations of the study.

Significance of the study.

Research methodology.

Chapter analysis.

Chapter Two: Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks and Literature Review:

Conceptual clarifications.

Theoretical and historical foundation.

Literature review.

Chapters Three and Four: These chapters are where students address the main topic, and the content and structure is flexible, although they usually form the largest part of the project.

For example, in a study of "The Analysis of Legal and Institutional Frameworks for Human Trafficking in Nigeria," Chapter Three could be: "Legal and Institutional Frameworks for Human Trafficking in Nigeria," and Chapter Four could be "Human Trafficking in Nigeria: Causes and Effects".

Chapter Five (or Six for PhD): Conclusion:

Summary of findings.

Recommendations.

Contribution to knowledge.

Areas for further studies.

Conclusion.

Note that under the doctrinal approach chapters one, two and the final chapter are presented the same way by all students, regardless of their topic, but the content may vary.

Non-Doctrinal Approach

The non-doctrinal approach has some differences in chapter structure:

Chapter One:

Background to the study.

Research hypothesis.

Purpose of the study.

Scope and limitation.

Significance of the study.

Synopsis of chapters.

Chapter Two: Literature review, theoretical and conceptual frameworks.

Chapter Three: Data collection and research methodology.

Chapters Four and Five: Data analysis, presentation of results, and discussions.

Chapter Six (for PhD): Conclusion, same as in doctrinal approach.

Preliminaries, Abstract, and Bibliography

The NALT guide specifies the content of the preliminaries and their numbering:

The Blank Fly Leaf

The Title Page

Approval page

Declaration

Certification

Dedication

Acknowledgement

Table of contents

List of tables

List of cases

List of statutes

Abstract

The abstract should be a concise summary of the research and its contents. It should highlight the research problem, methodology, key findings, and recommendations.

The bibliography, placed at the end of the research, should be a list of all materials consulted, whether cited in the text or not.

Key Formatting Points

Page Numbering: Page numbers are typically placed at the bottom centre of each page.

Chapter Starts: Each chapter should start on a fresh page.

Titles: All titles of preliminaries, items on the title page, and the table of contents should be in uppercase.

Practical Application

Let's consider an example of how a master's student would structure a project on "The Impact of Social Media on Defamation Law in Nigeria," using the doctrinal approach.

Chapter One: Introduction (Background, problem statement, objectives, etc.)

Chapter Two: Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks (Definitions of defamation, theories of free speech, etc., and a literature review of works on the topic).

Chapter Three: The Legal Framework for Defamation in Nigeria.

Chapter Four: The Impact of Social Media on Defamation Law.

Chapter Five: Conclusion (Summary of findings, recommendations, etc.).

Conclusion

The NALT format provides a clear and comprehensive framework for structuring legal research papers. By adhering to these guidelines, students and researchers can produce well-organized, coherent, and credible academic work. This guide should equip you with the tools to confidently structure various types of legal research papers, thereby enhancing the overall quality and impact of your research. The next blog post will focus on NALT citation guidelines for primary sources.

blogs.content:
The Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT) has developed a uniform format and citation guide designed specifically for legal research in Nigeria. This guide, often referred to as the NALT "Blue Book", aims to standardise legal writing and research within Nigerian tertiary institutions. It provides a consistent framework for citing legal sources, structuring research papers, and preparing articles for publication. This blog post will provide a detailed overview of the NALT citation style, its core principles, and how it adapts the OSCOLA (Oxford Standard for Citation of Legal Authorities) style.

Core Principles of the NALT Citation Style

The NALT citation style is designed to be user-friendly and relevant to the Nigerian legal context. It is an adaptation of the OSCOLA style with modifications to suit local legal materials and academic authors. The NALT guide was developed because of the lack of a uniform approach to legal research writing, which has had negative implications for legal education in Nigeria. The NALT guide addresses this by providing:

A dedicated citation guide: The NALT guide provides a dedicated citation guide to ensure uniformity and consistency in the citation of legal sources.

Minimal use of punctuation: NALT uses punctuation marks minimally, for example, it does not use full stops after abbreviations.

Localised examples: The NALT guide replaces foreign names, cases, and statutes with local examples where possible.

Footnote referencing: The NALT guide uses footnotes within the text for both citing sources and providing explanations.

Consistency: The NALT guide promotes a consistent and uniform approach to legal research writing across Nigerian tertiary institutions.

Key Features of the NALT Citation Style

The NALT citation style incorporates several key features that distinguish it from other citation formats. It adopts a footnote referencing system, meaning that citations are placed at the bottom of the page, rather than within the main text. Here are some specific features of the NALT style:

Minimal Punctuation: The NALT guide uses punctuation marks minimally. For example, no full stops come after abbreviations. "Laws of Federation of Nigeria" is abbreviated as LFN, and not L.F.N.

Case Names: In citing cases, "v" is used in place of "versus" or "vs" without a full stop. For example, Abacha v Fawehinmi is used rather than Abacha versus Fawehinmi. The case names should also be in italics, except for the "v" and the first letter of the names.

Footnote Numbers: Footnote numbers are indicated in-text by superscript Arabic numerals serially.

Author Names: In footnotes, the author’s name should be written exactly as it appears in the publication, omitting prefixes or titles, such as Mr., Mrs., Dr, Imam, Chief, Professor, Hon., Justice, Rev., Bishop, SAN.

Citing Multiple Sources: Where multiple citations are given in a single footnote, these should be separated by semi-colons.

Commas: Commas are used to separate the name of the author from the title of the work.

Colons: A colon is used to separate a title from a subtitle. For example, "Legal Research and Methodology: The A-Z of Writing Theses and Dissertations in a Nutshell".

Online sources: If a publication is sourced online, you should cite the hard copy version if it is available. If only the online version is available, the citation should include the web address in angle brackets, followed by the date of the most recent access.

Comparison with Other Citation Styles

While the NALT citation style draws inspiration from OSCOLA, it also has key differences from other widely used styles like MLA (Modern Language Association) and APA (American Psychological Association). Unlike MLA and APA, which use in-text citations (author-date system), NALT uses footnotes to provide bibliographic information. The NALT guide is also tailored to Nigerian legal resources and is less focused on international or multi-disciplinary sources. Here are some key differences in the NALT guide from other citation styles:

OSCOLA: NALT is adapted from the OSCOLA style, but with an emphasis on local content and authors.

MLA and APA: NALT differs significantly from MLA and APA, by using footnotes rather than in-text citations.

Why is NALT Important?

The NALT uniform format and citation guide is important because it addresses the lack of a uniform approach to legal research writing in Nigeria. It aims to achieve the following:

Standardisation: It standardises legal research and writing across Nigerian tertiary institutions.

User-Friendliness: It provides a user-friendly, indigenous citation guide for legal research in Nigeria.

Local Focus: It promotes the use of local authors and legal materials.

Clarity: It offers clarity and consistency in citation practices.

Facilitation of legal research: It facilitates the teaching of legal research methodology in higher institutions.

The NALT citation style provides a clear and consistent approach to citing legal sources.
